Assignment 2: Field-Level EDA Report

Summary: This report presents exploratory data analysis (EDA) comparing 30 agricultural fields across three growers in Iowa, Illinois, and Nebraska. The analysis covers field boundaries, CDL/cropland data (2021–2025), and NASA POWER weather data (2021–2025), focusing on the growing season (April–October).

1. Dataset Scope & Grower Locations

Three growers were analyzed, each with 10 fields in distinct agricultural regions:

Grower State County Fields Key Agricultural Feature
ia-grower Iowa (19) Kossuth 10 Northern corn belt, well-drained soils
il-grower Illinois (17) Iroquois 10 Eastern corn belt, high corn/soy yields
ne-grower Nebraska (31) York 10 Center-pivot irrigation over Ogallala Aquifer

2. Field Counts & Data Layers Used

Total dataset: 3 growers × 10 fields = 30 fields

  • Field Boundaries: GeoJSON polygons (EPSG:4326), original OSM data for IA/IL, synthetic for NE
  • CDL/Cropland Data Layer: 5 years (2021–2025) of crop type classifications per field; USDA data for IA/IL, synthetic for NE
  • Weather: NASA POWER daily data (2021–2025), 18,260 records per grower; filtered to growing season (Apr–Oct)
  • Soil Analysis: NOT INCLUDED — excluded per assignment requirements

3. Comparison Levels Used

Three nested comparison levels were applied across all analyses:

Level Description Example Analyses
Within-field (temporal) How a single field changes over time Crop rotation heatmap (5-year sequence)
Across fields (within grower) How fields differ within the same grower Field area vs. crop type; consistency vs. size
Across growers How growers differ across states Area distributions; temperature profiles; precipitation

4. Statistical Visualizations

Category A: Field Boundaries

Figure 1: Box and violin plots showing field area distributions by grower. Nebraska fields are largest on average, while Iowa fields are smallest and most uniform.
Figure 2: Grouped bar chart comparing total field count and combined acreage. All growers have 10 fields, but Nebraska has the largest total area (~1,625 acres).
Figure 3: Scatter plot of field area vs. dominant crop type (latest year). Corn and soybean fields show overlapping size ranges with no strong size bias by crop.

Category B: CDL / Cropland Data Layer

Figure 4a: Iowa crop rotation heatmap (field × year). Shows dominant crop per field over 5 years, revealing which fields rotate and which maintain consistent cropping.
Figure 4b: Illinois crop rotation heatmap. Similar temporal patterns with corn-soy rotation visible across multiple fields.
Figure 5: Stacked bar chart showing total acreage by crop type per grower. Nebraska has synthetic corn/soy data; Iowa and Illinois show more crop diversity (alfalfa, winter wheat).
Figure 6: Scatter plot of crop consistency (% years with same dominant crop) vs. field area. Pearson correlation shown; no strong relationship between size and rotation tendency.

Category C: Weather

Figure 7: Average monthly temperature during growing season (Apr–Oct). Nebraska is warmest, Iowa coolest; all show similar seasonal shape with July peak.
Figure 8: Mean cumulative precipitation during growing season. Nebraska is driest; Illinois and Iowa receive more rainfall, diverging mid-season.
Figure 9: Scatter plot of total growing season precipitation vs. average temperature. Pearson correlation and p-value shown; weak negative trend suggests cooler seasons may be wetter.

Category D: Geospatial Map

Figure 10: Geospatial map showing field polygon locations per grower. Each subplot shows the actual geographic spread of 10 fields within each state. Iowa fields are clustered near Kossuth County, Illinois fields span Iroquois County, and Nebraska fields are arranged in York County. Field IDs annotated at centroids.

5. Key Findings

  • Field Size: Nebraska fields are largest (~1625 total acres), Iowa smallest (~920 acres)
  • Temperature: Nebraska growing season is warmest (19.9°C avg), Iowa coolest (17.7°C)
  • Precipitation: Illinois receives the most growing season rainfall; Nebraska the least
  • Crop Rotation: Iowa and Illinois show diverse crop histories; Nebraska has synthetic corn/soy rotation
  • Correlations: No strong relationship found between field size and crop consistency, or between temperature and precipitation

6. Limitations, Missing Data & Assumptions

Nebraska CDL Data — Synthetic: The USDA NASS CDL server returned 503 errors for all Nebraska rasters (2021–2025). Synthetic CDL data was created with realistic corn/soy rotation patterns based on York County agricultural statistics. These files should be replaced with real USDA data when available.
Nebraska Field Boundaries — Synthetic: The OpenStreetMap Overpass API returned 406/503 errors. Field boundaries were created by translating Iowa geometries to York County, Nebraska. Shapes are rectangular approximations, not real-world field outlines.
  • Weather Scope: Only growing season (April–October) analyzed; full-year data available but not used
  • Correlation Method: Pearson r used; assumes linear relationships
  • Nebraska Heatmap: Skipped due to synthetic CDL format mismatch (documented in data notes)
  • Satellite/NDVI: Available in pipeline but excluded from this EDA focus

7. Confirmation: Soil Analysis Exclusion

Soil analysis was explicitly excluded from this assignment per requirements. SSURGO data was downloaded for all fields during pipeline execution (105 soil records for Nebraska, similar counts for Iowa/Illinois), but no soil visualizations or analyses were performed. Soil data remains available in the runtime for future use if needed.
